title: Chapter LIII

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter LIII,” how does Austen show Bingley returns? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter LIII, how does Austen develop the idea of Bingley returns? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LIII develops the idea of Bingley returns. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and plot shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter LIII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Bingley returns. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter LIII suggests about Bingley returns. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and plot), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter LIII to complicate the reader's understanding of Bingley returns. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of Bingley returns responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter LIII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of Bingley returns follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter LIII and its treatment of Bingley returns. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and plot, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter LIII as evidence for a larger claim about Bingley returns in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of Bingley returns. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

literaryElements.label: Characterization
literaryElements.explanation: Mr. Bennet mocks his new son-in-law ("He simpers, and smirks, and makes love to us all"); Mrs. Bennet, told Bingley is returning, insists she does not care while planning a dinner for him.

literaryElements.label: Irony
literaryElements.explanation: When Bingley and Darcy call, Mrs. Bennet is effusive to Bingley and coldly ceremonious to Darcy, the man who saved Lydia; Elizabeth alone knows the truth.

themesAndDevelopment.development: Mrs. Bennet's misplaced civility shames her daughters again, now in front of the man who rescued the family.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: silence and reserve
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: What characters leave unsaid (Darcy's reserve, Jane's composure, Elizabeth's secrets) drives misunderstanding. In this chapter: “seated by her; perhaps that was the reason of his silence; but it had not been so in Derbyshire. There he had” (Chapter LIII, paragraph 42).
symbolsAndMotifs.quote: seated by her; perhaps that was the reason of his silence; but it had not been so in Derbyshire. There he had

symbolsAndMotifs.name: letters
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Letters carry news, reveal character and change minds; Darcy's letter is the turning point of the novel. In this chapter: “Write to me very often, my dear” (Chapter LIII, paragraph 5).

Exemplar: The return of Bingley and Darcy turns the family's ignorance into painful dramatic irony. When the text says “Elizabeth particularly, who knew that her mother owed to the latter the preservation of her favourite daughter from irremediable infamy, was hurt and distressed to a most painful degree by a distinction so ill applied” (Chapter LIII, paragraph 41), it shows this directly. Mrs. Bennet greets Darcy coldly, but Elizabeth knows "her mother owed to the latter the preservation of her favourite daughter from irremediable infamy," so the reader feels the injustice of "a distinction so ill applied."

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
